## Introduction

This article is about where time and memory go when you run a dplyr pipeline
through cuplyr, and when to choose eager or lazy execution. It has numbers from
one machine, a list of cases where the GPU loses to plain dplyr, and advice
that follows from both. `vignette("query-optimization", package = "cuplyr")`
explains what the optimizer passes do. This one measures what they buy.

The short version: lazy, the default, is the better choice for pipelines,
though not because it is faster. With the memory pool cleaned before each run it
takes as long as eager or a little less up to 1e6 rows (2.53 against 2.66 ms at
1e3 rows, 2.85 against 2.99 ms at 1e6) and is slower on big tables: by 0.69 ms
at 1e7 rows and 0.98 ms at 5e7. (These are the README's numbers. The tables
below were timed with a plain `gc()` before each batch, which favours eager a
little: there the gaps are 0.67 ms at 1e7 and 1.0 ms at 5e7.) What it gives you
is that every intermediate column is freed when the pipeline finishes, so it
stays safe on big tables and in loops. In a loop an eager pipeline's leftovers
pile up, and once they fill the card cuplyr's out-of-memory handler has to run.
That made eager 3 to 7 times slower than lazy in the measurements below. Until
the card is full eager stays faster: in a separate run at 2.5e7 rows, five
back-to-back eager calls left about 4 GB behind and still took 9.2 ms each,
against 10 ms lazy.

```{r setup}
library(cuplyr)
library(dplyr)
```

## How a cuplyr call runs

Each verb call does some work in R (check the arguments, work out the new
schema) and then, in eager mode, some work on the GPU. At 1e3 rows the GPU part
is tiny and the R part dominates. A profile of one eager verb at 1e3 rows put
60 to 98% of the time on the R side: about 80% for `filter()`, `mutate()` and
`arrange()`, 98% for `select()` and 61 to 65% for a grouped `summarise()`,
whose GPU part is the biggest. That fixed cost is the per-call floor. At 1e3
rows it makes `filter()` and `mutate()` take as long as dplyr's, while
`select()`, `arrange()` and a grouped `summarise()` are faster than dplyr's
(see the per-call table below).

The two modes differ in when the GPU work happens.

- **Eager.** Each verb runs at once and returns a GPU table. Every
  intermediate table stays allocated until R's garbage collector drops it.
- **Lazy.** Each verb checks its arguments, works out the new schema and
  records a node in a plan, without touching the GPU. `compute()` optimizes the
  plan, runs it, and keeps the result on the GPU. `collect()` does the same and
  then copies the result to R. The intermediates are freed when the call
  returns.

Lazy is the default. You choose eager per table with
`tbl_gpu(df, lazy = FALSE)`, or for every table created afterwards with
`options(cuplyr.exec_mode = "eager")` (or the environment variable
`CUPLYR_EXEC_MODE=eager`; see `?"cuplyr-options"`). Printing a lazy table with pending steps runs the
plan to show its first rows and keeps nothing, so it costs about as much as a
`collect()` of the same plan (see the README for a measurement).
`show_query()` prints the pending steps of a lazy table. `explain()` prints them
next to the plan the optimizer will actually run:

```{r explain, eval = FALSE}
lazy <- tbl_gpu(mtcars) |>
  filter(mpg > 20) |>
  mutate(kpl = mpg * 0.425, hp2 = hp * 2) |>
  select(cyl, kpl)

explain(lazy)
#> Pending operations:
#> ast_select [2 cols]
#> | ast_mutate [2 expressions]
#> | | ast_filter [1 predicates]
#> | | | ast_source [11 cols]
#>
#> AST depth: 4
#> Node count: 4
#>
#> Optimized plan:
#> ast_select [2 cols]
#> | ast_mutate [1 expressions]
#> | | ast_select [2 cols]
#> | | | ast_filter [1 predicates]
#> | | | | ast_source [11 cols]
```

```{r explain-run, echo = FALSE}
# The output above is pasted so a default build shows it. A build with GPU
# evaluation runs the same code and fails if explain() no longer prints it.
lazy <- tbl_gpu(mtcars) |>
  filter(mpg > 20) |>
  mutate(kpl = mpg * 0.425, hp2 = hp * 2) |>
  select(cyl, kpl)
stopifnot(identical(
  trimws(capture.output(explain(lazy))),
  c("Pending operations:",
    "ast_select [2 cols]",
    "| ast_mutate [2 expressions]",
    "| | ast_filter [1 predicates]",
    "| | | ast_source [11 cols]",
    "",
    "AST depth: 4",
    "Node count: 4",
    "",
    "Optimized plan:",
    "ast_select [2 cols]",
    "| ast_mutate [1 expressions]",
    "| | ast_select [2 cols]",
    "| | | ast_filter [1 predicates]",
    "| | | | ast_source [11 cols]")
))
```

In the optimized plan the mutate has one expression instead of two, because
nothing uses `hp2`, and a select keeps only the 2 needed columns before the
mutate. Nothing has run on the GPU yet. `collect(lazy)` runs the plan.

The optimizer runs five passes when `compute()` or `collect()` is called:

- **Projection pruning** inserts a select that keeps only the columns the later
  steps need (the inner select in the plan above).
- **Mutate fusion** merges consecutive `mutate()` calls into one node, so they
  run as one step. It keeps the expressions in the order you wrote them, and
  it does not merge when the result would have more than 8 expressions or
  when the later `mutate()` reads more than 4 columns the earlier one creates.
- **Dead-column pruning** drops mutate outputs that nothing later uses (`hp2`
  above).
- **Filter pushdown** usually moves a filter below a mutate when the filter
  does not read a column that mutate computes, so the mutate sees fewer rows.
  It also moves filters below a `select()` that keeps their columns, and into
  the inputs of some joins. Whether a join allows it depends on its type and on
  its `relationship`, `multiple` and `unmatched` arguments; `explain()` shows
  where each filter ended up.
- **Filter reordering** usually merges consecutive `filter()` calls into one
  filter node, which builds one row mask and selects the rows once. It also
  sorts the merged predicates so the cheaper ones (estimated from the size of
  each expression) come first. Eager runs each `filter()` call on its own and
  allocates the filtered table in between.

A single `filter()` call with several predicates is already one filter node in
both modes: its predicates are combined with `&` into one expression. The
optimizer leaves their order alone unless it merges the call with another
filter. Some verbs, such as `arrange()` and
`summarise()`, are barriers: the passes run on each side of them but not
across.
`vignette("query-optimization", package = "cuplyr")` has the details.

## Measurements

Everything below is a static table. Nothing in this vignette is timed when it is
built. The code that produced the numbers is at the end.

- Date and code: 2026-10-26, cuplyr 0.1.1.9000, at the version that re-measured
  these tables (NEWS: "Faster eager verb calls"). The numbers of the version
  before it (NEWS: "Faster lazy verb calls", also measured on 2026-10-26) and of
  2026-10-23 (commit b39a8f1) are quoted where they are compared.
- Hardware and software: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 (12 GB), driver 615.78.08,
  R 4.6.1, dplyr 1.2.1. Memory resource `async` (the default).
- Method: data already on the GPU (uploads are not in the pipeline timings),
  warm, median of 15 samples (9 at 5e7 rows). Each sample timed a batch of
  calls fenced with `gpu_sync()`. The batch size came from one timed call and
  aimed at 30 ms, but the timer has 1 ms resolution, so batches of
  sub-millisecond calls ran anywhere from about 3 to 120 ms. Calls slower than
  30 ms ran one per batch. R's `gc()` ran, untimed, before every batch. Each
  number in the tables is the median of three fresh R processes. The three runs
  differed by up to 4% for the cuplyr pipelines, by up to 5% for dplyr's
  pipeline at 1e6 rows, by up to 9% for the sub-millisecond calls, by up to 7%
  for the two 1e3-row transfers (0.13 and 0.10 ms) and by up to 10% for the
  optimizer case at 1e7 rows. At 1e3 and 1e6 rows the 1 ms clock and that
  spread put a gap of 0.1 ms between eager and lazy inside the noise; "Reading
  the table" has a finer timing of the two.
- Some figures in "Reading the table" come from separate profiling runs, one
  or two of them, not from the three runs behind the tables. The text says so
  where they appear.

### A five-verb pipeline

```r
filter(x > 0.1) |> mutate(z = x * y + w) |> group_by(g) |>
  summarise(m = mean(z), n = n()) |> arrange(desc(m)) |> collect()
```

The table has an integer `g` with 100 groups and double columns `x`, `y` and
`w`. The dplyr column runs the same pipeline on a tibble. "Held" is how much
GPU memory the call leaves allocated until R's next `gc()`, measured as the
growth of `gpu_memory_state()$pool_used_bytes` across one call whose result is
collected.

| rows | eager ms | lazy ms | dplyr ms | eager held MB | lazy held MB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1e3 | 1.87 | 1.75 | 3.50 | 0.04 | 0 |
| 1e6 | 2.00 | 2.00 | 22.0 | 32 | 0 |
| 1e7 | 4.33 | 5.00 | 213 | 324 | 0 |
| 5e7 | 17.5 | 18.5 | not run | 1620 | 0 |
| 5e7, 5 calls back to back, no `gc()` | 68.4 | 18.0 | not run | | |

The last row is what a loop or a script does: it runs the pipeline five times
without a `gc()` in between and reports the mean time per call. It shows the
cautious end of a range. The eager figure depends on what the memory pool already
holds. In two earlier runs of the same five-call loop (commit b39a8f1) it was
145 and 155 ms per call, against 22 and 24 ms for lazy.

### One eager verb at 1e3 rows (the per-call floor)

No `collect()`. The result stays on the GPU.

| verb | cuplyr ms | dplyr ms |
|---|---|---|
| filter | 0.36 | 0.35 |
| mutate | 0.37 | 0.39 |
| select | 0.10 | 0.42 |
| arrange | 0.14 | 0.68 |
| grouped summarise | 0.40 | 0.77 |

### Transfers (4 columns)

| rows | `tbl_gpu()` upload ms | `collect()` of all rows ms |
|---|---|---|
| 1e3 | 0.13 | 0.10 |
| 1e6 | 6.00 | 6.00 |
| 1e7 | 63.0 | 54.0 |

### A case built for the optimizer

A 21-column table (`g` plus `x1` to `x20`), one query that computes columns it
later drops and filters after the mutate:

```r
mutate(a = x1 * 2, b = x2 * x3, c = x4 + x5) |> filter(x1 > 0.9) |>
  select(g, a) |> collect()
```

`explain()` shows the optimizer reading 2 of the 21 columns at the source,
running the filter below the mutate, and dropping `b` and `c`.

| rows | eager ms | lazy ms | dplyr ms | eager held MB | lazy held MB |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1e6 | 1.73 | 1.73 | 22.5 | 43 | 0 |
| 1e7 | 6.20 | 4.86 | 183 | 428 | 0 |

### Reading the table

- With clean GPU memory, lazy is as fast as eager or a little faster up to 1e6
  rows and slower above that. At 1e3 rows it took 1.75 ms against 1.87 for
  eager, and at 1e6 rows 2.00 against 2.00. With the 1 ms clock both gaps are
  inside the noise (see the method). Timed with longer batches (0.15 s each,
  11 samples taken in turns, three fresh processes) lazy took 1.75 to 1.76 ms
  against 1.87 to 1.88 at 1e3 rows, and 1.95 to 1.98 ms against 2.05 to 2.08
  at 1e6: 4 to 6% shorter. At 1e7 rows lazy is 0.67 ms behind (5.00 against
  4.33 ms, 15% longer) and at 5e7 rows 1.0 ms (18.5 against 17.5 ms, 6%).
  Before the lazy verb calls were changed (NEWS: "Faster lazy verb calls") the
  gaps at 1e7 and 5e7 rows were 1.2 and 1.5 ms. On 2026-10-23 they were 1.0 ms
  at 1e3 and 1e6 rows, 2.4 ms at 1e7 and 3.0 ms at 5e7.
- Where the time goes at 1e3 rows, from two separate profiling runs:
  recording the five-verb plan takes 1.0 ms, all of it work in R.
  `collect()` of the recorded plan takes 0.66 ms: 0.04 ms to optimize it,
  0.43 ms to lower and run it, 0.09 ms to copy the result to R and the rest
  bookkeeping. The eager pipeline takes 1.85 to 1.87 ms in all. Before this
  version recording took 2.07 ms and `collect()` 0.80 ms, and before the lazy
  verb calls were changed (NEWS: "Faster lazy verb calls") 2.7 ms and about
  1.2 ms. A lazy verb no longer infers the schema of the whole pending plan
  again, the optimizer and the lowering infer each node's schema once, the
  optimizer recognises in one walk a plan its passes would leave as it is (this
  one), and each verb call now walks its expression fewer times. Recording time
  does not depend on the row count.
- Why lazy is slower on big tables, from a separate profiling run: at 1e7 rows
  recording takes the same 1.0 ms and `collect()` of the recorded plan 3.8 ms,
  of which 3.6 ms is lowering the plan and running it on the GPU. The
  optimizer changes nothing in this plan (`explain()` shows the same five
  steps before and after), so both modes run the same five GPU steps. The
  difference is overlap. An eager verb returns while its GPU work is still
  running, so the next verb's R work runs at the same time. Lazy does its R
  work first, while the GPU waits, and then runs the steps back to back. Making
  eager wait for the GPU after every verb shows how much that is worth: in three
  runs eager took 4.25 to 4.33 ms, 5.14 to 5.17 ms with a `gpu_sync()` after
  every verb, and lazy 5.00 ms. Without its overlap eager is slower than lazy,
  so lost overlap accounts for all of lazy's 0.67 ms. The overlap grows with
  the GPU work, which is why the gap appears only on big tables. (Earlier
  versions of this article said overlap explained little of the gap. That
  measurement called `gpu_sync()` before each verb instead of after it.)
  Lazy's GPU step, which frees its intermediates when it returns, adds about
  0.05 ms at every size.
- The optimizer makes lazy faster than eager in the case built for it, but only
  on the bigger table: 4.86 against 6.20 ms at 1e7 rows (22% shorter). At 1e6
  rows the two tie at 1.73 ms, because there is too little GPU work for the
  skipped work to matter. Lazy held nothing in both cases, eager held 43 and 428
  MB.
- Extending a lazy plan costs the same however long it already is, and
  `collect()` takes time in proportion to the plan's length. In a separate
  profiling run, adding a `filter()` or `mutate()` to a lazy table took 0.16 to
  0.19 ms at every length from 1 to 100 verbs. Before this version it took
  0.5 ms, and before the lazy verb calls were changed 0.6 ms on 1 verb, 16.5 ms
  on 50 and 64 ms on 100. `collect()` of a 100-verb plan of `mutate()` calls
  took 8.8 ms, against 9.5 before this version and 53 before that. The exception
  is a join: recording one on a plan of 120 nodes took about twice as long as
  on a plan of 3 (0.61 against 0.30 ms; 0.84 to 0.87 against 0.30 to 0.31
  before this version).
- Memory is the reason to prefer lazy. Here an eager pipeline leaves about 32
  bytes per row behind until R's next `gc()`: 324 MB at 1e7 rows, 1620 MB at
  5e7. Run it again before the `gc()` and the memory pool keeps growing. In a
  traced run of the five-call loop it went from 5.4 to 11.6 GB on a 12 GB card,
  and then cuplyr's out-of-memory handler ran `gc()` and `gpu_gc()` and retried
  the step. This is what happens in the back-to-back row: 68.4 ms against
  18.0 ms, lazy 3.8 times faster. The two earlier runs gave 6.6 and 6.7 times.
- Before the card fills, eager stays faster. In a separate run at 2.5e7 rows
  (not part of the tables), five back-to-back eager calls left about 4 GB
  behind and took 9.2 ms each, against 10 ms lazy.
- Against dplyr on a tibble at 1e3 rows both modes are ahead (1.87 ms eager and
  1.75 ms lazy against 3.50 ms, 1.9 and 2.0 times faster). At 1e6 rows cuplyr
  is 11 times faster, and at 1e7 rows 43 to 49 times.

## Where the GPU loses

- **Tiny tables.** At 1e3 rows a single cuplyr call takes 0.10 to 0.40 ms,
  most of it R-side work, and the GPU gives no gain on `filter()` and
  `mutate()`: they take as long as dplyr's (0.36 and 0.37 ms against 0.35 and
  0.39). `select()`, `arrange()` and the grouped `summarise()` are faster than
  dplyr's, by 4.2, 4.8 and 1.9 times. A whole pipeline at that size is 1.9 to
  2.0 times faster than dplyr (1.87 ms eager and 1.75 ms lazy against 3.50 ms),
  so the gain is small in absolute terms: under 2 ms per pipeline.
- **Transfers.** Moving data costs more than the compute. Uploading 1e7 rows
  takes 63 ms and collecting them 54 ms, against 4.33 ms for the eager
  pipeline. If you upload, run one cheap verb and collect, the GPU loses.
- **CPU fallbacks.** Some expressions have no GPU translation, and cuplyr
  evaluates them in R instead, copying data across. This is silent by default.
  Set `options(cuplyr.fallback = "warn")` to be told when it happens, or
  `"error"` to forbid it. The message names the verb, the expression, the
  reason and how much data was copied. A lazy plan that has to run early (a
  `summarise()` of `mean(x * y)`, say) stays on the GPU and is a different
  thing, a plan break: `options(cuplyr.plan_break = "warn")` reports it, and
  it never errors. `?"cuplyr-fallback"` has the details.

## Practical advice

- Upload once and keep the data on the GPU between steps. Collect once, at the
  end of the pipeline.
- Use lazy for pipelines, most of all on big tables and in loops, where not
  holding intermediates matters. Do not expect it to be faster on a big table:
  with clean GPU memory it was level with eager or a little faster up to 1e6
  rows and 0.67 to 1.0 ms slower at 1e7 and 5e7. It wins when an eager
  pipeline's leftovers pile up.
- Use eager for interactive exploration and single calls where you want each
  result at once.
- To branch from a shared prefix, `compute()` it once and build the branches
  from the result. It keeps the table on the GPU.
- After dropping a large eager result, `gc()` frees it back to cuplyr's memory
  pool, where the next calls reuse it. `gpu_gc()` does that too and then returns
  the pool's unused memory to the card, so other processes can use it. It takes
  about a second and the next calls have to grow the pool again, so use it when
  you need the memory elsewhere, not inside a loop.
  `vignette("memory", package = "cuplyr")` covers the memory resources and when
  memory is freed.
- Fence GPU timings with `gpu_sync()`. GPU calls return before the kernels
  finish, so a timer without it may stop the clock before the GPU work is
  done.
- Check `explain()` when a lazy pipeline is slower than you expect. See
  `vignette("query-optimization", package = "cuplyr")` for the passes.

## Reproduce

This is a trimmed copy of the script behind the tables, covering the pipeline
timings and the memory column. It is not run when the vignette is built. Run it
in a fresh session on an idle GPU. It sizes each batch from one timed call
that the 1 ms timer resolution rounds, so batches of sub-millisecond calls can
run well under or over the 30 ms it aims for.

```{r reproduce, eval = FALSE}
library(cuplyr)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1)

# Median ms per call. A sample is a batch of calls fenced with gpu_sync();
# gc() runs untimed before every batch.
per_call <- function(fn, samples = 15, warmup = 3, target = 0.03) {
  for (i in seq_len(warmup)) fn()
  gpu_sync(); gc(verbose = FALSE)
  t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]; fn(); gpu_sync()
  one <- max(proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0, 1e-4)
  reps <- max(1L, min(500L, as.integer(ceiling(target / one))))
  t <- vapply(seq_len(samples), function(i) {
    gc(verbose = FALSE)
    t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
    for (j in seq_len(reps)) fn()
    gpu_sync()
    (proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0) / reps
  }, numeric(1))
  1e3 * median(t)
}

# GPU memory one call leaves allocated until R's next gc(), in MB.
held_mb <- function(fn) {
  gc(verbose = FALSE); gc(verbose = FALSE); gpu_sync()
  u0 <- gpu_memory_state()$pool_used_bytes
  r <- fn(); gpu_sync()
  u1 <- gpu_memory_state()$pool_used_bytes
  rm(r)
  (u1 - u0) / 1e6
}

pipeline <- function(d) {
  d |>
    filter(x > 0.1) |>
    mutate(z = x * y + w) |>
    group_by(g) |>
    summarise(m = mean(z), n = n()) |>
    arrange(desc(m))
}

n <- 1e6
df <- data.frame(g = sample.int(100L, n, TRUE), x = runif(n), y = runif(n),
                 w = rnorm(n))
tb <- tibble::as_tibble(df)
eg <- tbl_gpu(df, lazy = FALSE)
lz <- tbl_gpu(df, lazy = TRUE)

c(eager = per_call(function() collect(pipeline(eg))),
  lazy  = per_call(function() collect(pipeline(lz))),
  dplyr = per_call(function() pipeline(tb)))
c(eager = held_mb(function() collect(pipeline(eg))),
  lazy  = held_mb(function() collect(pipeline(lz))))
```
